summary: A best current practice describing how IRTF research groups are formed and run, and how their participants relate to the IRSG and the IAB. It covers the procedures, not any technical protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: The IRTF (Internet Research Task Force) runs small, long-lived groups that study research questions about the Internet. RFC 2014 says how such a group is set up, what its charter must contain, how it meets, who does what, and how it is shut down if it stops making progress. It is a process document: it describes no technical protocol.

subtitle: How IRTF research groups are formed, run and closed, and who does what.

tldr.problem: The IRTF needed a shared description of how its long-term research groups are chartered, run and ended, and how they relate to the IRSG and the IAB.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets out a five-part charter reviewed by the IRSG and approved by the IAB, light operating guidelines, a termination path, and duties for each role.
tldr.outcome: It gives research groups wide freedom: no consensus requirement, optional limited membership, and success judged by research quality and impact.

today: RFC 2014 is a Best Current Practice, BCP 8, published in October 1996. The unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes IRTF procedures as of that date and is based on RFC 1603.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The document defines guidelines and procedures for Internet Research Task Force Research Groups. The IRTF focuses on longer term research issues related to the Internet, while the parallel organization, the Internet Engineering Task Force, focuses on the shorter term issues of engineering and standards making.

The Internet is a loosely-organized international collaboration of autonomous, interconnected networks. It supports host-to-host communication through voluntary adherence to open protocols and procedures defined by Internet Standards, a collection commonly known as the TCP/IP protocol suite. The IRTF is composed of a number of focused, long-term, small Research Groups working on topics related to Internet protocols, applications, architecture and technology. Research Groups are expected to have the stable long term membership needed to promote the development of research collaboration and teamwork in exploring research issues. Participation is by individual contributors, rather than by representatives of organizations.

The IRTF is managed by the IRTF Chair in consultation with the Internet Research Steering Group. The IRSG membership includes the IRTF Chair, the chairs of the various Research Groups and possibly other individuals, members at large, from the research community. The IRTF Chair is appointed by the IAB, the Research Group chairs are appointed as part of the formation of Research Groups, and the IRSG members at large are chosen by the IRTF Chair in consultation with the rest of the IRSG and on approval by the IAB.

Except for members at large of the IRSG, there is no general participation in the IRTF, only participation in a specific Research Group. The document uses shall, will, must and is required for steps that are essential, and suggested, should and may for guidelines that are not essential but are strongly recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: The IRTF is the research arm of the Internet standards community. It works through small groups on longer-term questions, while the IETF handles shorter-term engineering and standards work. This document explains how those research groups are formed and run, and who is responsible for what.

sections.title: The IRTF Approach
sections.content:
The IRTF does not set standards, and thus has a different and complementary philosophy and procedures. An IRTF Research Group is expected to be long-lived, producing a sequence of products over time. The products of a Research Group are research results that may be disseminated by publication in scholarly journals and conferences, as white papers for the community, as Informational RFCs, and so on. It is also expected that technologies developed in a Research Group will be brought to the IETF as input to Working Groups for possible standardization. However, Research Group input carries no more weight than other community input, and goes through the same standards setting process as any other proposal.

Research Groups are formed to encourage research in areas of importance to the evolution of the Internet. Anyone may conduct such research, whether or not they are members of a Research Group. The expectation is that by sponsoring Research Groups, the IRTF can foster cross-organizational collaboration, help to create critical mass in important research areas, and add to the visibility and impact of the work.

Research Groups may have open or closed memberships. Limited membership may be advantageous to the formation of the long term working relationships that are critical to successful collaborative research, but it must be used with care and sensitivity to avoid unnecessary fragmentation of the work of the research community. Allowing limited membership is in stark contrast to IETF Working Groups, which are always open. To ameliorate the effects of closed membership, all Research Groups are required to regularly report progress to the community, and are encouraged to hold occasional open meetings, most likely co-located with IETF meetings. The IRTF may host open plenaries at regular IETF meetings. The work of the IRSG is expected to be marked by informality, because the goal is to encourage valuable research, not to add burdensome bureaucracy.
sections.plainLanguage: Research groups do not write standards. They produce research results, which may later be offered to the IETF as input, where they get exactly the same treatment as any other proposal. A research group may keep its membership closed, which the IETF never does, and it can still report progress openly.

sections.title: Research Group Formation
sections.content:
Research Groups are the activity centers in the IRTF. A Research Group is typically created to address a research area related to Internet protocols, applications, architecture or technology.

A Research Group may be established at the initiative of an individual or group of individuals. Anyone interested in creating one must submit a charter for the proposed group to the IRTF Chair along with a list of proposed founding members. The charter will be reviewed by the IRSG and then forwarded to the IAB for approval. If approved, the charter is placed on the IRTF Web site and published in the Internet Monthly Report.

In determining whether it is appropriate to create a Research Group, the IRTF Chair, the IRSG and the IAB will consider several issues. Is the research area that the group plans to address clear and relevant for the Internet community? Will the formation of the group foster work that would not be done otherwise, for instance membership drawn from more than a single institution or country? Do the group's activities overlap with those of another Research Group, which may still be appropriate but must be considered carefully, since subdividing efforts often dilutes the available technical expertise? And is there sufficient interest and expertise in the topic, with at least several people willing to expend the effort likely to produce significant results over time?

Research Groups require considerable effort, including management of the group process, editing of group documents and contribution to the document text. IRTF experience suggests that these roles typically cannot all be handled by one person, and that at least four or five active participants are typically required. A proposal to create a Research Group should therefore include a list of potential charter members. The IAB will also review the charter to determine the relationship of the proposed work to the overall architecture of the Internet Protocol Suite.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can propose a research group by sending the IRTF Chair a charter and a list of founding members. The IRSG reviews it and the IAB approves it. The proposal has to show a clear and relevant topic, that the work would not happen anyway, and that enough people are willing to do the work: usually four or five active participants, because editing and chairing take time too.

sections.title: The Research Group Charter
sections.content:
A charter is a contract between a Research Group and the IRTF to conduct research in the designated area. Charters may be renegotiated periodically to reflect changes to the current status, organization or goals of the group. The formation of a Research Group requires a charter, initially negotiated between a prospective Research Group Chair and the IRTF Chair, which becomes the basis for forming the group once both are satisfied with its form and content.

The charter consists of five sections. The Research Group Name should be reasonably descriptive or identifiable, and the group shall define an acronym, at most 8 printable ASCII characters, to reference the group in the IRTF directories, mailing lists and general documents. The name and acronym must not conflict with any IETF names and acronyms. The Chair(s) section names one or two chairs to perform the administrative functions of the group, with their email addresses. The Mailing list(s) section gives an address for members of the community to send queries, such as requests to join the group, and an interest list open to all interested parties for open discussion and announcements; it should also give the subscription procedure and the location of the archive. The group may also have a list limited to regular meeting participants, on which much of the work is likely to be conducted by email.

The Membership Policy section must define whether membership is open or limited and the procedure to apply, though limited membership is in no way encouraged or required. The Description of Research Group section sets out the focus and intent briefly, so that by reading it alone a person can decide whether the group is relevant to their own work. Its first paragraph must give a brief summary of the research area, basis, goals and approaches, and will frequently be used as an overview of the group's effort. The charter shall also describe the proposed research and discuss objectives and expected impact with respect to the Internet Architecture.
sections.plainLanguage: The charter is the group's contract with the IRTF, and it has five parts: the name and a short acronym, the chairs, the mailing lists, the membership policy, and a description of the research. The description has to be enough for a reader to tell at a glance whether the group is relevant to them.

sections.title: Research Group Operation
sections.content:
Research Groups are autonomous and each determines most of the details of its own operation with respect to session participation, reaching closure, norms of behavior and so on. Since the products are research results and not Internet standards, consensus of the group is not required. The measure of success is the quality and impact of the research results.

For coordinated, structured interactions, the Chair must publish to the group mailing list a draft agenda well in advance of the actual meeting. The agenda needs to contain the items for discussion, the estimated time necessary per item, and a clear indication of what documents participants will need to read beforehand. A Research Group conducts much of its business via its electronic mail distribution lists, and is also likely to meet periodically for things better done interactively, such as brainstorming and heated altercations. Meetings may be telephone conference, video teleconference or face-to-face meetings. It is strongly encouraged that all Research Group meetings be recorded in written minutes, which should include the agenda, an account of the high points of the discussion and a list of attendees, and which should be sent to the interest group and made available through the IRTF Web and ftp sites.

Each Research Group determines the balance of email and face-to-face meetings appropriate for making progress on its goals. Electronic mail permits the easiest and most affordable participation, while face-to-face meetings often permit better focus, more productive debate and enhanced working relationships. Face-to-face meetings are encouraged to be held co-located with the regular IETF meetings to minimize travel and to encourage the cross-fertilization that occurs during hallway and after-hours interactions. The challenge to managing meetings is to balance the need for consideration of the various issues against the need to allow forward progress, and the Research Group as a whole has final responsibility for striking this balance.
sections.plainLanguage: A research group runs itself. It does not have to reach agreement, and success is judged by the quality of the research, not by votes. The chair must send an agenda out well before each meeting, listing the items, the time each will take and the papers to read first, and should write up the minutes afterwards.

sections.title: Termination, Staff Roles and Documents
sections.content:
If it becomes evident that a Research Group is not making progress in the research areas defined in its charter, or fails to regularly report the results of its research to the community, the IRTF Chair can, in consultation with the group, require that the group recharter to refocus on a different set of problems, request that the group choose new chairs, or disband the group. If the Research Group disagrees with the IRTF Chair's choice, it may appeal to the IAB.

The IRTF Chair is responsible for ensuring that Research Groups produce coherent, coordinated, architecturally consistent and timely output as a contribution to the overall evolution of the Internet architecture. The Chair monitors the range of activities, coordinates the work done by the various Research Groups, reports on IRTF progress to the IAB and the wider Internet community, and tracks the progress of the groups with the aid of a regular status report from the Research Group chairs. IRSG members advise the IRTF Chair on the chartering of new Research Groups and on other matters relating to the smooth operation of the IRTF, and most of them are also Research Group chairs.

The Research Group Chair is concerned with making forward progress and has wide discretion in the conduct of group business. The Chair must ensure that a number of tasks are performed, either directly or by others assigned to the tasks: ensuring the group process and content management, moderating the group email list so that discussions stay relevant and do not devolve into flame attacks, organizing and chairing meetings, ensuring that minutes are taken, distributing the work among the participants, and coordinating document publication with the RFC Editor. Process management pertains strictly to the style of the group's interaction and not to its content, and the secretarial function encompasses preparation of minutes and possibly editing of group-authored documents. Taking minutes and editing jointly-authored documents is often performed by a specifically designated participant or set of participants.

The work of a Research Group usually results in research papers and other documents, as well as documents in the Informational or Experimental RFC series, which is the archival publication record for the Internet community. The RFC series is a publication mechanism only, and publication does not determine the status of a document: status is determined through separate, explicit status labels. All Internet Standards are published as RFCs, but not all RFCs specify standards. Authors are expected to work with the RFC Editor to meet all formatting, review and other requirements, and initial publication as an Internet Draft is preferred in all cases. All relevant documents for a meeting, including the final agenda, should be published to the group mailing list and available at least two weeks before a meeting starts.
sections.plainLanguage: If a group stops making progress, the IRTF Chair can make it recharter, ask it to pick new chairs, or disband it. The group can appeal to the IAB. Each role has duties: the IRTF Chair coordinates, IRSG members advise, and the group chair keeps the process moving, moderates the mailing list, shares out the work and shepherds the documents towards publication as RFCs.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Security issues are not discussed in this memo. The document deals with the way research groups are chartered and run, not with the protocols they study, so it leaves the security questions of those protocols to the specifications that describe them.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo does not discuss security. It says so in one sentence and moves on.

viz.caption: THE FIVE SECTIONS OF A RESEARCH GROUP CHARTER

items.title: Research Group Name
items.text: A descriptive name plus an acronym of at most 8 printable ASCII characters that must not clash with any IETF name.

items.title: Chair(s)
items.text: One or two chairs to run the group's administration, with their email addresses.

items.title: Mailing list(s)
items.text: An address for queries, an open interest list for everyone, and possibly a list for regular participants.

items.title: Membership Policy
items.text: Whether membership is open or limited, and the procedure to apply for it.

items.title: Description of the Group
items.text: The focus and intent, so that a reader can tell whether the group is relevant to their own work.
